claims.text: Increasing Cr or Al content in a multiprincipal-element alloy enhances oxidation resistance during high-temperature oxidation.
Increasing Cr or Al content improves material integrity during high-temperature oxidation.
The oxidation-resistance improvement arises from formation of a continuous, adherent, and slowly growing protective oxide scale.
The baseline alloy is homogenized and has a uniform elemental distribution with a moderate concentration of the protective element.
Increasing the concentration of a critical oxide-forming element promotes formation of a continuous and adherent surface scale.
The protective scale is primarily composed of Cr2O3 or Al2O3.
A higher concentration of the oxide-forming element promotes its segregation to the alloy surface at high temperature.
Surface enrichment in the oxide-forming element produces a self-healing oxide layer.
The resulting oxide layer has low diffusivity and retards oxygen ingress.
Retarding oxygen ingress preserves the integrity of the underlying alloy.
Relative to the baseline, the enriched alloy will have a lower oxidation rate and reduced mass gain.
Relative to the baseline, the enriched alloy will form a thinner and more coherent oxide scale.
Relative to the baseline, the enriched alloy will retain its mechanical properties better after oxidation.
The proposed behavior is expected to hold during isothermal oxidation at approximately 800–1100 °C.
At substantially lower temperatures or under extreme oxidation conditions, alternative degradation mechanisms may dominate and the hypothesis may not apply.
Qualitative trends supporting the hypothesis have been observed in related alloy systems.
